cards.front: The germ theory of disease says that many diseases are caused by {{c1::microbes}} that get into the body.
cards.quote: The germ theory of disease says that many diseases are caused by microbes that get into the body.
cards.section: Explain: germ theory, and the test in Vienna

cards.front: A microbe or virus that causes disease is a {{c1::pathogen}}.
cards.quote: A microbe or virus that causes disease is a pathogen.
cards.section: Explain: germ theory, and the test in Vienna

cards.front: In the Vienna clinic data, how is a death ratio calculated, and why use it?
cards.back: Deaths divided by the number of women counted, times 100. It lets clinics of different sizes be compared.
cards.quote: A death ratio is deaths divided by the number of women counted, times 100, so clinics of different sizes can be compared.
cards.section: Explain: germ theory, and the test in Vienna

cards.front: {{c1::Pasteurization}} heats a food such as milk for a set time to kill harmful bacteria.
cards.quote: Pasteurization heats a food such as milk for a set time to kill harmful bacteria.
cards.section: Explain: germ theory, and the test in Vienna

cards.front: Why is a disinfectant such as chlorine not the same as sterilization?
cards.back: Chlorine kills many microbes on surfaces, but some bacterial spores survive. Sterilization removes all forms of microbial life from an object.
cards.quote: Destroying microbes: disinfectants such as chlorine kill many microbes on surfaces, though some bacterial spores, tough resting forms of certain bacteria, survive.
cards.section: Explain: germ theory, and the test in Vienna

cards.front: If the First Clinic's examiners' hands carried the cause of childbed fever, which clinic's ratio should fall once washing starts, and to about what level?
cards.back: The First Clinic's, toward the Second Clinic's level of about 3 per 100. It fell from 18.27 in April 1847 to 2.24 in June.
cards.why: Washing removes the cause only for the clinic whose examiners carried it.
cards.quote: If the examiners' hands carried the cause, which clinic's ratio should fall once washing starts, and to about what level?
cards.section: Explain: germ theory, and the test in Vienna

cards.front: Why is the First Clinic's full year of 1848 a fairer after-washing comparison than the single month of June 1847?
cards.back: Single months varied: the First Clinic's monthly ratio was about 2 to 5 per 100 from December 1846 to March 1847, before the April rise. A full year averages out that swing.
cards.quote: so the full year 1848 is a fairer after-washing comparison than any one month.
cards.section: Where the Vienna numbers come from

cards.front: In 1846 the First Clinic recorded 459 deaths among 4,010 women and the Second Clinic 105 deaths among 3,754. Which clinic had the higher death ratio, and about how many times higher?
cards.back: First: 459 / 4,010 x 100 = 11.45 per 100. Second: 105 / 3,754 x 100 = 2.80 per 100. The First was about four times higher.
cards.quote: In every year shown before 1847, which clinic had the higher death ratio?
cards.section: Explain: germ theory, and the test in Vienna

cards.front: What does a vaccine do for the immune system, and what does it avoid?
cards.back: It teaches the immune system to recognize a pathogen without causing the full disease.
cards.quote: A vaccine teaches the immune system to recognize a pathogen without causing the full disease.
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: A vaccine works through an {{c1::antigen}}, a substance the immune system can recognize, often a protein on a pathogen's surface.
cards.quote: It works through an antigen, a substance the immune system can recognize, often a protein on a pathogen's surface.
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: {{c1::Antibodies}} are proteins that stick to one antigen and help destroy or block it.
cards.quote: The response includes antibodies, proteins that stick to one antigen and help destroy or block it.
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: What do memory B cells do when the antigen from an earlier vaccine shows up again?
cards.back: They recognize the antigen quickly, multiply, and turn into cells that make large amounts of antibody.
cards.quote: Later, memory B cells recognize the antigen quickly, multiply, and turn into cells that make large amounts of antibody.
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: What is in a toxoid vaccine, and what are two examples?
cards.back: A bacterial toxin (a poison some bacteria make) made harmless. Tetanus and diphtheria vaccines are examples.
cards.quote: A bacterial toxin, a poison some bacteria make, made harmless
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: The MMR vaccine protects against measles, mumps and rubella. What kind of vaccine is it, and what does it contain?
cards.back: A live weakened vaccine: a weakened form of the virus or bacterium.
cards.quote: A weakened form of the virus or bacterium
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: What does an mRNA vaccine deliver to the body's cells, and what do the cells do with it?
cards.back: It delivers instructions that the cells use to make one viral protein.
cards.quote: Instructions your cells use to make one viral protein
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: In a made-up model, microbes double every 12 hours from a start of 1 until the defense arrives. How much smaller is the peak if the defense arrives on day 3 (memory cells ready) instead of day 7 (a first meeting)?
cards.back: Day 7 allows 14 doublings (about 16,000 microbes); day 3 allows 6 (64). Four days earlier is 8 fewer doublings, and 2 multiplied by itself 8 times is 256: a peak 256 times smaller.
cards.quote: Four days earlier means eight fewer doublings, and 2 multiplied by itself eight times is 256: a peak 256 times smaller.
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: In the doubling model, unwashed hands pass on 100 microbes and washed hands pass on 1. About how many doublings is the 100-fold difference worth, and how many days at two doublings a day?
cards.back: About 6.5 doublings, since 2 multiplied by itself 6 or 7 times gives 64 or 128. At two a day that is about 3 days.
cards.quote: Suppose unwashed hands pass on 100 microbes and washed hands pass on 1.
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: Besides memory cells, why does a vaccinated person often stop a microbe before it multiplies?
cards.back: Some antibody-making cells live for years and keep making antibody, so antibody is already waiting. A small share of vaccinated people still get measles.
cards.quote: Some antibody-making cells live for years and keep making antibody, so a vaccinated person often has antibody waiting to block a microbe before it multiplies.
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: Why do antibiotics that hit bacteria mostly spare your own cells?
cards.back: Your cells have no cell wall, and their ribosomes differ enough from bacterial ribosomes that these drugs mostly leave them alone.
cards.quote: Why does it spare you? Your cells have no cell wall.
cards.section: What the second film left out

cards.front: Name the four ways, listed by the CDC, that bacteria resist an antibiotic.
cards.back: Letting less drug in, pumping it out, breaking it down, or changing or bypassing the target.
cards.quote: The CDC lists four ways: letting less drug in, pumping it out, breaking it down, or changing or bypassing the target.
cards.section: What the second film left out

cards.front: A drug kills every sensitive bacterium in an infection of 10 billion (10^10). One in 100 million (10^8) is resistant. How many survive, and about how many doublings bring them back to 10 billion?
cards.back: 10^10 / 10^8 = 100 survivors. Every 10 doublings multiply a number by about 1,000, so about 27 doublings bring 100 back to 10 billion.
cards.quote: Every 10 doublings multiply a number by about 1,000 (2 multiplied by itself 10 times is 1,024), so about 27 doublings bring 100 back to 10 billion.
cards.section: What the second film left out

cards.front: A person with a cold, which a virus causes, takes an antibiotic. What happens to the virus, and how can this still add to resistance?
cards.back: Nothing happens to the virus. The drug still kills harmless sensitive bacteria in the body, which leaves room for resistant ones.
cards.quote: The drug does nothing to the virus, but it still kills harmless sensitive bacteria in your body. That leaves room for resistant ones.
cards.section: What the second film left out

cards.front: Resistance can already be present, arise as a new DNA change, or pass as a gene from another bacterium. Why does the drug raise the share of resistant bacteria in every case?
cards.back: It kills the sensitive bacteria and leaves the resistant survivors to multiply. This is natural selection.
cards.quote: Either way, the drug favors the survivors: natural selection
cards.section: What the second film left out

cards.front: Why might the true number of measles infections in the United States before 1963 be higher than the reported counts?
cards.back: The CDC estimates 3 to 4 million people were infected each year, but only about 500,000 cases a year were reported.
cards.quote: Before then, the CDC estimates, 3 to 4 million people in the United States were infected each year, though only about 500,000 cases a year were reported.
cards.section: Elaborate: from two clinics to a nation

cards.front: What did it mean when measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000?
cards.back: No continuous spread inside the country for at least 12 months. It did not mean zero cases.
cards.quote: Measles was declared eliminated in 2000, meaning no continuous spread inside the country for at least 12 months, not zero cases.
cards.section: Elaborate: from two clinics to a nation

cards.front: CDC records list 481,530 reported U.S. measles cases in 1962 and 22,231 in 1968. A measles vaccine became available in 1963. By about what factor did reported cases fall?
cards.back: 481,530 / 22,231 is about 21.7, so reported cases fell about 22 times. These are reported cases, not all infections.
cards.quote: These are reported cases from the CDC's historical measles dataset; a vaccine became available in 1963.
cards.section: Elaborate: from two clinics to a nation

cards.front: A company has a new vaccine against a made-up disease that spreads in schools. Design a fair test: groups, what you count, and what result would show it works.
cards.back: Chance assigns volunteers to the vaccine or a look-alike placebo shot, so the groups tend to be alike. Count confirmed cases in each group, defined before the trial. Keep dose schedule, follow-up time and illness checks the same, and blind volunteers and judges. Far fewer cases in the vaccine group supports the vaccine; similar numbers mean no clear effect.
cards.why: Thousands of volunteers are needed so enough cases occur to compare.
cards.quote: chance assigns volunteers to the vaccine or a look-alike placebo shot, which tends to make the groups alike in age, health and habits.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the doubling model, which does more to shrink the peak: a 100-fold smaller starting number of microbes, or a defense that arrives 4 days earlier? Which real practice is each?
cards.back: The 4-day head start does more: 8 doublings is 256 times, while 100-fold is about 3 days. The smaller start is hygiene such as washing; the earlier defense is a vaccine.
cards.quote: that is about 3 days, so in this model a 100-fold smaller start does the same as a defense arriving about 3 days earlier.
cards.section: Explain: vaccines, a head start in the race

cards.front: For a bacterial infection and a viral infection in the race model, which of hygiene, vaccination and an antibiotic could help, and which fails against the virus?
cards.back: Hygiene shrinks the start and a vaccine moves the defense earlier, in both. An antibiotic works only on sensitive bacteria, so it helps against the bacterial infection but fails against the virus.
cards.quote: Hygiene shrinks the start, a vaccine moves the defense earlier, and an antibiotic works only on sensitive bacteria.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking
